newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Colombian coffee exporters look for added value.
newsitem.headline: Colombian coffee exporters look for added value.

text.p: Colombia needs to tap into the value added side of the global coffee market if it wants squeeze more profit out of its world-class beans, the head of an influential trade group said.
"We need to increase the added value of our coffee so that the country can fetch a higher price," said Gabriel Rosas, president of the National Coffee Exporters Association (Asoexport).

Rosas, who will preside over Asoexport's 60th annual assembly later this week in Cartagena, said Colombia was basically losing out on the lion's share of the profit to be made in the global marketplace by limiting itself to little more than the growing and shipping of green beans.
Providing the raw material is one thing, and Colombia's excelso beans fetch well-deserved premiums because of their excellent quality.
But Rosas said Asoexport estimates that up to 87 percent of the profit in coffee today is in roasting, trading, commercialization -- and even advertising.

Colombians are barred from some of those activities by strict controls that date back more than 70 years, he added, saying it was time for the tightly-regulated industry to cut the red tape preventing it from moving where the money is.
Even the contracts that exporters are required by the government and National Coffee Growers Federation are in need of a major overhaul, Rosas said.

He said the contracts require exporters to provide roasters with a fixed amount of coffee over a set time period. But they allow for no change in prices if these should swing upwards at anytime during the life of the contract, meaning exporters are essentially barred from taking advantage of price volatility.
"That assymetry has to be eliminated because it doesn't suit the purpose of improving marketing conditions to provide advantages for just one of the protagonists," Rosas said.

Rosas, who spoke to reporters Tuesday night, said he was providing a sneak preview of what promises to be some of the leading discussion items at the three-day annual assembly opening in Cartagena Thursday.

Underscoring the fact that the National Growers Federation -- and its long adherence to government regulations -- is likely to come under pressure for change at the meeting, he said it could no longer seek to control the industry single-handedly.
"The federation has played an extraordinary role over a long time period, but it can't do everything itself," he said.
